business: Albany County Fasteners (Raw Products Corp), Edison, NJ
opportunity: Quote-desk agent: RFQ intake to priced, documented quote for B2B and custom/off-catalog requests (audit.md opportunity #1)

problem.summary: Every B2B quote at Albany County Fasteners is assembled by hand by a small salaried sales team inside a roughly 20-person family firm. The company advertises quotes for listed and unlisted products, USA sourcing, custom manufacturing, blanket release and stock-and-lock programs, plus C of C / MTR / shop-drawing packets, and sells in piece, pack and bulk tiers with no order minimum. Each request therefore means catalog lookup, tier-price math, a stock check and document assembly, often while purchasing, fulfillment, QC and marketing each sit on a single family member. Public evidence of the workflow is on the B2B Request-A-Quote page and the company's own About page; volumes and minutes per quote are not public and remain assumptions in the audit.

current_tools.evidence: Storefront page source carries Shopware theme tokens and CMS element markup; profile tech footprint records Shopware 6 with bulk pricing configured in the platform and order history in the account portal.

current_tools.evidence: The B2B page lists custom quotes for listed and unlisted products, documentation on request, and an online NET 30 credit application; requests are handled by the in-house sales team.

current_tools.tool: Tawk.to live chat widget on the storefront
current_tools.evidence: Profile tech footprint records the Tawk.to chat widget toggled from header and footer during weekday business hours.

current_tools.tool: Phone line 866-573-0445 and email, staffed Monday-Friday 8:00AM-5:00PM EST
current_tools.evidence: Contact page publishes the toll-free number, email and Edison address; About page publishes weekday 8-5 EST hours with no after-hours coverage.

current_tools.tool: Unnamed 'AI-powered Warehouse Management System' for real-time inventory and fulfillment
current_tools.evidence: About page says the company uses a smart, AI-powered WMS for real-time inventory and automated workflows; the product is not named publicly, so its API is unknown.

current_tools.tool: Amazon storefront as a second sales channel
current_tools.evidence: Profile records an Amazon storefront alongside the own store, meaning two catalogs and two price surfaces to keep aligned.

solution.design: A private quote-desk service that sits beside the existing Shopware 6 store and the sales inbox. Inbound RFQs arrive by web form, email or PDF; a parser turns each into structured line items (thread size/pitch, length, grade/material, finish, quantity, unit of measure). A retrieval step matches each line against the live Shopware catalog (product number, attributes, pack quantity) and reads the applicable price for the customer's group and quantity tier. Deterministic code, not the model, does the arithmetic: extension, tier selection, minimums, freight table. The model drafts the quote document and, where requested, assembles a C of C / MTR packet from the client's existing spec sheets, citing the catalog row behind every price. The draft lands in a rep queue as an editable PDF preview plus a line-level source table. Nothing is emailed to a customer by the agent: a rep approves, edits or rejects, and the approved document is sent from the rep's own mailbox and logged. Unlisted, custom-manufactured, blanket-release and stock-and-lock requests are routed as exceptions with the sourcing questions pre-drafted for the purchasing manager. Every draft, edit and approval is logged for later measurement and for the company's own sub-0.5% order-error objective. Deliberate exclusions in v1: no payment data, no credit decisions, no autonomous sending, no Amazon catalog writes.

components.component: RFQ intake and document parsing (email, PDF, form, photos of a parts list)
components.tool: Postmark inbound email webhook + custom Python parser calling an OpenAI multimodal model
components.why: Postmark delivers inbound mail as a webhook with attachments, so the service needs no mailbox credentials; the model handles messy buyer formats that rule-based parsing misses.

components.tool: Shopware 6 Admin API (OAuth integration credentials, POST /api/search/{entity})

components.why: Cheap enough that inference is a few dollars a month at this volume; a stronger model can be reserved for hard lines. The vendor-hosted model means customer RFQ text leaves the building, so a self-hosted open-weight option is the fallback if the client objects.
Renders the client's existing quote layout and merges C of C/MTR pages without a per-document licence; runs on the same small server.

components.why: Gives the reps a filterable queue with a status column and edit history; the free tier covers a pilot's quote volume without a custom admin UI.

Optional later channel; API/webhook behaviour not verified in this research, so chat is out of the v1 scope

solution.human_in_the_loop: A named rep is the only sender. The agent produces a draft quote PDF plus a line-level source table (catalog row, price rule, stock snapshot, exception flags). The rep approves, edits or rejects each draft in the queue; unlisted, custom-manufactured, blanket-release, stock-and-lock, government/DFARS and any line with an unresolved part match are mandatory exceptions that cannot be auto-approved. Refusals in v1: no autonomous customer email, no price overrides, no credit terms, no refunds, no catalog writes. The approval event (user, timestamp, diff) is written to an append-only log so the client can audit any quote that leaves the building.

steps: Collect read-only Shopware integration credentials, a catalog export, the price-tier rules and two or three representative customer price agreements
Collect 50-100 recent RFQs and the quotes actually sent in reply, plus blank and completed C of C/MTR samples
Walk the quote desk in Edison with the sales lead and time 20 live requests end to end
phases.client_provides: API credentials, price rules, historical RFQs and sent quotes, document templates, one approver and one purchasing contact, two hours of walkthrough time

steps: Pull the active catalog and normalize fastener attributes (thread, length, grade, material, finish, drive, pack quantity) into a searchable index
Extract the piece/pack/bulk ladder and customer-group prices; build a test set of 200 SKUs with known correct prices
Verify one real quote's arithmetic against the index before writing any generation code
phases.client_provides: Confirmation of tier logic and any unpublished customer-specific overrides; a 30-minute review of the price test set

steps: Parse email bodies, PDFs and form submissions into structured line items with units
Match lines to catalog products, return candidates with confidence and flag ambiguous or unlisted items
Score the parser against the historical RFQs; iterate on the worst 20 failures
phases.client_provides: Answers on 20 sample lines where the buyer's meaning is ambiguous; a list of common misspellings and shorthand buyers use

phases.phase: Phase 4 - Draft quote, certificate packet and approval queue
steps: Render the quote in the client's layout with per-line source citations
Assemble C of C/MTR packet pages from existing spec sheets, with the lot/cert reference left for the rep
Build the approval queue, exception rules and append-only approval log
Add guardrails: no send capability, scoped API keys, redaction of any payment fields, prompt-injection handling for attachments
phases.client_provides: Branded quote template, approved boilerplate terms, certificate templates, list of who may approve

steps: Run the agent in shadow mode on live listed-part RFQs for four weeks while reps work normally
Compare each draft to the quote the rep actually sent; log line matches, price differences, edit reasons and minutes
Weekly 30-minute review with the sales lead; tune exceptions and retrieval
phases.client_provides: A rep to approve and score drafts, roughly 15 minutes a day, and access to the sent-quote record

steps: Deliver runbook, escalation rules, monitoring and a monthly accuracy report template
Hand over credentials, repository and a restore-tested backup; agree the monthly care scope
phases.client_provides: A named internal owner for the tool and a decision on the monthly care plan

pilot.scope: One workflow, one channel set, listed parts only: web RFQ form plus the quote email inbox. The agent drafts the quote and the C of C/MTR packet in shadow mode; the rep compares each draft to the real quote and approves. Unlisted, custom-manufactured, blanket release and stock-and-lock requests are captured but routed to a human without a draft, so the pilot does not touch the hardest sourcing work.
pilot.weeks: 4 weeks of shadow running (plus 4-6 weeks of build before it)
success_metrics: Line identification accuracy on listed parts: at least 85% of lines matched to the correct SKU without rep correction
Price traceability: 100% of quoted lines show a catalog row and price rule, with zero unexplained prices
Draft usefulness: at least 50% of drafts approved with no change to line items or prices
Handling time: median minutes per quote reduced by at least 40% versus the timed baseline
Exceptions: at least 95% of unlisted/custom lines correctly flagged and kept away from auto-draft
Safety: zero customer-facing documents sent by the agent; zero price overrides without a logged rep approval
pilot.baseline_method: Before build, the sales lead times 20 live requests end to end with a stopwatch and logs each step (lookup, price math, document assembly, review). The same 20 requests are then replayed through the agent, and the pilot compares each live draft to the quote the rep actually sent from the sent-quote archive. Minutes are compared as medians, not averages, so one unusually large RFQ does not distort the result.
pilot.exit_criteria: Proceed to production if line accuracy is at least 85%, price traceability is 100%, median handling time falls at least 40%, and no unapproved document reached a customer. Stop and refund the unused pilot fee if accuracy stays below 70% after two tuning rounds, if the client cannot supply price rules or historical quotes, or if the WMS/stock source cannot be read reliably enough to avoid stale stock claims.

Rounded up for retries, PDF/photo parsing and weekly eval runs.
DigitalOcean Basic Droplet, 2 GiB memory / 1 vCPU, listed monthly price
Postmark Pro, 10,000 emails per month including inbound processing; overage USD 1.30 per 1,000

WeasyPrint is open source and runs on the same droplet; the custom Python service has no per-seat licence

suggested_pricing.pilot_fee: USD 2,500 for the 4-week shadow pilot (credited in full against the set-up fee if the client proceeds)
suggested_pricing.setup_fee: USD 5,000 one-time for catalog/price indexing, RFQ parser, quote and certificate templates, approval queue, guardrails and handover
suggested_pricing.monthly_fee: USD 750 per month for care (monitoring, accuracy reporting, exception tuning, one small change per month, business-hours support)
suggested_pricing.reasoning: INFERENCE, reasoned against competitor and labour anchors rather than the consultancy's track record, which does not exist yet. (1) Competitor floor: Qotora sells a comparable distributor quote agent at USD 149-799/month with setup included, and QuoteWerks sells quote authoring at USD 15-30/user/month, so a monthly fee above roughly USD 800 invites a like-for-like comparison the consultancy loses on price and maturity. (2) Competitor ceiling: AY Automate starts at USD 3,000/month and Shopware's own B2B quoting tier starts at EUR 2,400/month, which leaves room for a mid-priced, Shopware-specific build. (3) Labour anchor: a loaded NJ order clerk is about USD 4,820/month (USD 46,270 median x 1.25 / 12), so USD 750/month is roughly one-sixth of a hire. (4) Value anchor: the audit estimates USD 13,900-41,700/year of clerical time, i.e. about USD 1,160-3,475/month. USD 750/month is about 65% of the low-end monthly benefit and about 22% of the high-end; pilot plus setup (USD 7,500) equals about 54% of one year's low-end benefit and about 18% of the high-end. That is defensible only because the pilot is measured against a timed baseline rather than the audit's assumptions. (5) The certificate-packet assembly and Shopware-native integration are the parts Qotora does not advertise, which is what the premium over USD 349/month buys.

leverage.point: The Shopware 6 Admin API, with OAuth integration credentials and a generic /api/search/{entity} pattern, is reusable across every Shopware B2B distributor, so the same connector can be sold again with configuration rather than new code.

The open-source stack (WeasyPrint rendering, a small Python service, a Baserow queue) has no per-seat or per-document licence, so a second and third client can be served from the same codebase at near-zero marginal software cost.

Qotora's published plans show a real, priced market for distributor quote automation at USD 149-799/month and confirm the human-approval, price-traceability pattern, which validates a shared core and gives a reference price for future pitches.

Fastener attribute normalization (thread, grade, finish, pack quantity) is the reusable domain asset: the same normalizer applies to any fastener, industrial or MRO distributor, and it is the piece generic quote tools handle worst.

The client's existing tools do not need replacing - Shopware stays the system of record and the reps keep their mailbox - so there is no migration to sell, and the same sidecar pattern fits other Shopware merchants.

Local presence: the consultancy is in Milltown and the warehouse is in Edison, so on-site walkthroughs, in-person document handover and same-day drop-ins are practical in a way they are not for a remote SaaS vendor.

edge_vs_competitors: Real but narrow. The edge is (a) Shopware-native reading of the actual catalog and customer price tiers instead of a generic ERP/database connector, (b) C of C/MTR document assembly tied line-by-line to the quote, which Qotora does not advertise and Shopware's own quote objects do not attempt, (c) a private single-tenant deployment on the client's own small server with no per-quote metering, no multi-tenant data mixing and a written no-training arrangement, and (d) local, in-person delivery with a fixed-price measured pilot. The consultancy has no edge on price against Qotora (USD 149-799/month with setup included), no edge on brand or references, no 24/7 support organisation, no fastener-industry case studies and no ERP breadth. A buyer who only wants email-to-quote drafting will rationally pick Qotora; the pitch has to be the certificate packet, the private deployment and the willingness to sit in the Edison office.

risks_compliance.issue: Quote accuracy and certificate integrity. A wrong grade, alloy, finish or pack quantity on a quote, or an inaccurate C of C/MTR, is not a cosmetic error - the Fastener Quality Act makes it a violation to knowingly falsify or misrepresent a lot's record of conformance, characteristics, markings or manufacturer's insignia.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Fastener Quality Act, 15 U.S.C. 5401 et seq.; NIST compliance FAQ on misrepresentation and record of conformance
risks_compliance.mitigation: Deterministic price math, per-line catalog citation in every draft, mandatory rep approval before any customer-facing document, and a hard rule that certificate pages are assembled only from the client's own spec sheets with lot/cert references filled by a person.

risks_compliance.issue: Government/defense quotes: specialty-metal sourcing certifications (domestic melt) may be required on fasteners sold into DoD contracts, and the COTS exception does not automatically cover fasteners.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: DFARS 252.225-7009, Restriction on Acquisition of Certain Articles Containing Specialty Metals
risks_compliance.mitigation: Flag any government end-use or flowdown clause at intake, never let the agent assert domestic-melt status, and route those lines to purchasing for certification before the quote leaves.

risks_compliance.issue: ITAR-controlled drawings or technical data. If a customer sends controlled defense drawings for a custom part, handling them can trigger DDTC registration and export-control obligations; uploading them to a third-party model API could be a deemed export.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: 22 CFR 122.1, registration requirements for manufacturers/exporters of defense articles and furnishers of defense services
risks_compliance.mitigation: Explicit intake rule that ITAR/export-controlled drawings are refused by the agent and escalated to a person; no third-party model processing of such files; self-hosted model option if the client has any controlled work.

risks_compliance.issue: Prompt injection and tool abuse through inbound RFQ emails and PDF attachments (instructions hidden in a document trying to make the agent change prices, email someone, or leak data).
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
risks_compliance.mitigation: Agent has no send capability and no price-write capability, tool allowlist, attachments treated as untrusted data, outputs validated against the catalog before display, and every draft human-approved.

risks_compliance.issue: Customer and contact data privacy under the New Jersey Data Privacy Act, in force since January 2025, which applies to controllers meeting consumer-volume thresholds.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: P.L. 2023, c.266 (S332): applies at 100,000 consumers, or 25,000 consumers plus revenue from selling personal data; 'consumer' excludes a person acting in a commercial context
risks_compliance.mitigation: Most data handled is business contact and order data, which falls outside the Act's 'consumer' definition, and the thresholds are unlikely to be met; still minimize retention, keep logs on the client's own server, and confirm annual consumer counts in discovery.

risks_compliance.issue: Model-vendor data handling: whether RFQ content and prices are retained or used for training by the model provider, and whether the client's customer price agreements permit that.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: No rule confirmed; depends on the API terms in force at contract time
risks_compliance.mitigation: Use an API tier with no-training/limited-retention terms in writing, redact unnecessary customer detail, and offer a self-hosted open-weight model for clients who refuse third-party processing. Terms must be re-checked before signature.

risks_compliance.issue: Platform drift: Shopware upgrades or a change in the client's price-rule configuration can silently break retrieval and produce stale prices.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Shopware Admin API documentation (versioned endpoints; behaviour tied to the instance version)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Scoped read-only integration credentials, version pinning, a nightly regression test against a fixed set of 200 known SKUs and prices, and an alert if a price lookup returns nothing.

risks_compliance.issue: Single-founder delivery risk: no staff, no 24/7 cover, and a pilot that overlaps with a day job.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Not a legal rule; commercial risk from the consultancy's own structure
risks_compliance.mitigation: One workflow, one client, fixed four-week shadow scope, business-hours support commitment stated in the contract, documented runbook and a kill switch the client controls.

risks_compliance.issue: Overstating savings. The audit's USD 13,900-41,700 range rests on assumed request volume and handling minutes, and public data confirms neither.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Audit assumptions (50-100 requests/week x 50 weeks x 30 minutes x 40-60% pre-built) and the NJ order-clerk wage basis
risks_compliance.mitigation: Quote the range as an estimate, measure a timed baseline in week one, and contract the pilot on measured minutes rather than the audit's numbers.

feasibility.weeks_to_pilot: 10-12 weeks from signed pilot to measured pilot result (4-6 weeks build part-time, then 4 weeks shadow running)
feasibility.reasoning: Technical 3/5: the Shopware Admin API is documented and OAuth-scoped, the cost stack is trivial (roughly USD 35-50/month), and the quote document itself is a rendering problem, not a research problem. What holds it at 3 is the matching layer - fastener nomenclature across 40M+ pieces, piece/pack/bulk tiers, customer-group prices and a WMS whose API is unknown - plus the certificate packet, which needs the client's own spec sheets and a human for lot references. Commercial 4/5: the pain is documented on the client's own B2B page, the decision-maker is reachable, the benefit range (USD 13,900-41,700/year) supports a USD 750/month fee, and there is one workflow with a measurable baseline. It is not a 5 because Qotora already sells a credible version of this at USD 149-799/month with setup included, so the consultancy must win on Shopware specificity, certificate assembly and local private deployment rather than on being the only option. Conditions: (a) the client supplies read-only API credentials, the tier-price rules and 50+ historical RFQs before build starts; (b) the pilot is scoped to listed parts and shadow mode, with no autonomous sending; (c) the WMS stock source is resolved or the agent explicitly labels stock as a snapshot; (d) the engagement is contingent on a timed baseline showing at least 15 minutes of handling per quote, since below that the savings case collapses.

discovery_questions: How many quote or documentation requests arrive per week, and what share are listed parts versus unlisted or custom-manufactured?
Which WMS are you running, and can it expose stock by API or scheduled export? Is Shopware stock the same number your reps trust?
Where do your piece/pack/bulk tiers and any customer-specific price agreements live - in Shopware price rules, a spreadsheet, or in the reps' heads?
Which quote format do buyers actually receive today: a PDF, a portal link, or an email body? Can you share three examples, including one C of C/MTR packet?
Who approves a quote before it goes out, and is there a discount or price-override limit a rep can apply without a second signature?
How often do you attach C of C, MTR or shop drawings, and who pulls those documents today?
Do you quote into government or defense buyers where DFARS specialty-metals or domestic-melt certification applies?
Do you ever receive ITAR or export-controlled drawings, and how are those handled now?
How is freight estimated on a quote - a table, a UPS rate lookup, or rep judgement?
What is the actual number of quotes the sales team sends in a normal month (this decides the plan tier and the fee), and what is the median minutes per quote?
Would you accept a single-tenant deployment on a server you control, and do you have a policy on sending customer RFQ text to a third-party AI provider?
Who is the internal owner for this tool after handover - sales, purchasing, or IT?
caveats: All founder-day estimates, token volumes and cost ranges are inferences from list prices and the audit's assumed volumes; none has been validated against the client's actual data.
The audit's impact range (USD 13,900-41,700/year) depends on 50-100 requests/week, 30 minutes per quote and a 40-60% pre-built share, all of which are explicitly assumptions, not measurements.
